title: Introducing Versori by Avalara
summary: Versori Joins Avalara to Scale AI-Native Integration Infrastructure for Global Commerce
body_text: Versori Joins Avalara to Scale AI-Native Integration Infrastructure for Global Connectivity MANCHESTER, U.K., March 2, 2026 Versori, a next-generation integration platform built to automate connector development using agentic AI workflows, today announced it has joined the Avalara, Inc. family, the global leader in tax compliance automation. The deal validates Versori’s vision of transforming how enterprise integrations are built and maintained through AI-driven automation. By joining Avalara, Versori will accelerate the deployment of its technology across one of the world’s largest compliance ecosystems, enabling thousands of commerce, ERP, and financial systems to connect faster and operate with greater reliability. Founded to solve the growing complexity of enterprise integrations, Versori developed a platform that automates connector development and maintenance using agentic AI. The result is dramatically faster integration delivery, simplified lifecycle management, and infrastructure that scales globally without sacrificing reliability. ‍ “From the beginning, our mission at Versori has been to integrate the world’s most complex enterprises,” said the Versori co-founders. “Joining Avalara allows us to bring that vision to a global platform where integration accuracy and uptime are mission-critical for compliance and commerce.” ‍ Versori’s automation-first architecture enables organisations to build and maintain integrations across complex system landscapes, including ERPs, ecommerce platforms, marketplaces, and financial systems, with significantly reduced development overhead. Its agentic AI workflows automate much of the traditionally manual work involved in building and updating connectors, allowing integrations to adapt as systems evolve. By integrating Versori’s technology, Avalara will accelerate its ability to scale integrations across thousands of commerce platforms while advancing its broader strategy to deliver real-time, always-on compliance within every transaction. ‍ "Compliance at global scale depends on seamless, reliable integration," said Scott McFarlane, CEO and Co-Founder of Avalara. "Versori's technology and team significantly accelerate our ability to connect into the world's commerce systems quickly, at scale using intelligent, AI-driven automation that meets the reliability and accuracy standards global compliance demands. This acquisition strengthens our unified platform and advances Avalara's vision of AI-native compliance that operates continuously, intelligently, and at scale across the world's most trusted commerce systems." ‍ As part of the acquisition, Versori’s founders and team will join Avalara to continue advancing integration automation and agentic AI capabilities. The platform will operate as Versori, by Avalara, expanding integration capabilities across Avalara’s global compliance ecosystem. With the backing of Avalara, Versori’s technology will now power integrations at a scale previously impossible, bringing autonomous integration infrastructure to the systems that run global commerce. ‍

Anne Rice’s The Vampire Lestat Q&A – Mark Johnson, Hannah Moscovitch & Daniel Hart on The Creative Journey to Season 3
summary: We sat down with executive producer Mark Johnson, showrunner Hannah Moscovitch, and composer/writer Daniel Hart to discuss everything from this season’s unique creative process to some of the unexpected musical inspirations that influenced this season.
body_text: In Anne Rice’s The Vampire Lestat , Lestat de Lioncourt has reinvented himself as The Vampire Lestat, a rock musician keen on telling his side of the story. While on tour and being haunted by the “muses” from his past, his band’s popularity grows and so does Lestat’s influence over vampires and humans alike. We sat down with executive producer Mark Johnson, showrunner Hannah Moscovitch, and composer/writer Daniel Hart to discuss everything from this season’s unique creative process to some of the unexpected musical inspirations that influenced this season. So, I was trying to think of a way to visualize for audiences what the three of you do and how your work flows together, and I came up with this. If The Vampire Lestat is a living thing — Mark oversees the outer layer; Hannah is in charge of the meat, the muscle, and Daniel is in charge of the blood. Does that ring true to you? Mark Johnson: I’ll be the blood and the guts! [ Laughs ] Hannah Moscovitch: I think this year though, Daniel did so much and so many things. He was in the writer’s room, composing the songs, composing the score, and was on set making sure that the band looked right playing their musical instruments and performing, and that the music was authentic. You were doing a lot of things! Daniel Hart: Yeah, true. HM: So maybe he’s more like the organs. [Laughs] DH: It might be that Lestat is my blood actually. Thinking about it now, yes! We are each other’s blood. It’s a symbiotic relationship. DH: Indeed! So, Daniel, we spoke in June of 2024 about Season 2 and at that point you had started working on the music for this season. We talked a little about inspiration back then, and also about your process of working with Rolin for guidance. You were doing things scene by scene for Season 2, but obviously for The Vampire Lestat you were writing songs way before scenes were written. Can you talk a little about your creative process for this season? DH: I wrote the majority of the songs in the writer's room starting in 2024. That made it easier for me because we could sit around the table for a while and talk about character, talk about story arcs and plot points. We could talk about who was coming back this season from previous seasons and who was coming into this season who hadn't been there before. We talked about the key things we wanted to bring in from the books and what were things that we felt like we had some liberties to be creative with in terms of the story that Anne had created. So, all that was data for me that I could take and go off and work on songs related to that. I felt like I had been given a good foundation when I started working on songs, but then the songs came pretty quickly, faster than I thought they would, which probably says something about the blood being shared between me and Lestat. They were just simmering and waiting to come out. DH: I guess that says something about how much I relate to that character in ways that I didn't think that I did. HM: Or it just says something about how talented you are! DH: Oh, Hannah. [ Laughs ] So yeah, the songs came faster than the scenes coming out of the writer's room so that meant that everybody who was writing scenes had to figure out ways to work the songs into scenes. I had written lyrics that would no longer make sense after we figured out exactly who a character was going to be and what their relationship would be to Lestat, so then I would go back and revise lyrics. Or we would make songs longer or shorter based on the length of a scene. There was plenty of that, a lot of back and forth, but it was easier than I thought it would be to get to these songs and get to the essence of who Lestat is this season and who he has been in the past. How to reflect that in lyrics especially and in the music that he wanted to make for this season. When it comes to artistic and fashion influences, Lestat has his feet firmly planted in some of the coolest decades. I immediately thought of Marc Bolan, but I also thought of Scott Weiland of the Stone Temple Pilots and Gavin Rossdale in those early Bush years. Definitely a bit of a 90s vibe in there. DH: Very much so. When you were sorting out vibe, look, aesthetics how did you land on decisions? And I know I’m not off on the Bolan reference because you know I picked up on the use of ‘Jewel’ by T. Rex in Episode 3 immediately! DH: Yes! Well, we knew that Lestat was going to go on this huge journey of self-discovery throughout the season and that made me immediately feel like he can't stay in one genre or style of music. If he's evolving, then the music needs to evolve as well. It would have been my personal preference anyway because I like writing in lots of different styles of music and I don't like pigeon-holing myself or being pigeon-holed, so that was a fun challenge for me to figure out what styles he would be exploring. I had a conversation with Rolin [Jones, creator] early on in the writer's room. I said, "Does Lestat listen to Beyoncé and does he like her?" And Rolin was like, "Yeah, of course he listens to Beyoncé because everybody listens to Beyoncé!" So no, personally, I don't think Lestat’s music is overtly influenced by Beyonce's music. I feel like he's on a different journey, he's a different being. He's been around for 265 years! He saw orchestras play in 18th century France, so it's a different set of influences for Lestat. So, we figured out as we went along what his stylistic evolution would be. There's absolutely some T. Rex and Bowie in there, but all the way up to Chappell Roan, Mitski, and Olivia Rodrigo. There was a song that I was writing, and I went and listened to an Olivia Rodrigo song just to make sure I wasn't unintentionally stealing from someone else! [ Laughs ] There was also 100% a song where we were almost done with it, we were mixing it. Danny Reisch is the co-producer of all these songs with me this season, and he also mixes all the orchestral music too for the score. So, Danny and I were in his studio together and we were listening back to one of the songs from this season, and I said, "Can we make this sound a little bit more like a Stone Temple Pilots song?" I feel so validated! So, thank you [ laughs ]. Hannah, you’ve been in the thick of it in the writer’s room since the beginning. You're an incredibly prolific playwright which seems on its surface like such an independent venture that wouldn’t necessarily set you up for the teamwork needed in a writer’s room – but obviously that’s not the case. What has it been like being with this crew from the start of this crazy adventure, and how has your role shifted and changed as the seasons have progressed? HM: In Season 1, I was in the writer’s room only, so I wasn't on set at all. I was a producing writer but just in the room, so I was there for five months and then I was there for a couple of weeks in the Fall that year when we had to rebreak the whole season. So, I did that with Rolin, lived in his office house, but then from then on, I've been on the show also in production and throughout production. So that was a big shift, and I've been doing that since Season 2. MJ: She’s almost always by a camera. So, if Rolin's back in the writer’s room or doing whatever he's doing, Hannah's right on top of not just protecting the script, but quite frankly, the entire thing. And just a note, Rolin believes in — completely believes in — and I think is most comfortable with playwrights, which is very rare for most TV showrunners. I've worked with several who won't have a playwright anywhere near the role! HM: I am a playwright and I think part of the reason why I was able to come onto this show is because there is a similarity between my voice and Rolin's voice, and we both do things in a similar way. We like things to go dark, we like things to be grounded but operatic. We like humor and different levels of humor. We like the mix of dark and funny, so ultimately, we have an affinity and we can really write with each other. If you're walking down the streets of your favorite city with your headphones on, what do you put on to strut your stuff? MJ: It depends on that city and what time of day it is. So really it can be anything. I listen to a lot of opera and don't know anything about opera, but I find it incredibly fulfilling. Beyond that, I don't know. You? HM: I listen to some angry girl music. For sure, I love some of that, but I listen to a million different things. I listen to whatever I've heard recently that I most love, so yeah, it's hard to say one thing because I think I’m eclectic. I listen to really weird, different things. DH: ‘St. Thomas’ by Sonny Rollins. I knew Daniel would have a specific answer immediately! title: New poll reveals how Americans feel towards asylum seekers following Supreme Court ruling
summary: Americans base asylum support on why someone flees, not where they're standing, and opinions shifted after hearing the SCOTUS ruling. Learn more.
body_text: On June 25th, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado that migrants waiting on the Mexican side of an official border crossing haven't legally "arrived" in the United States, and therefore aren't entitled to apply for asylum. Writing for the majority, Justice Alito drew a line between "arriving at" the border and "arriving in" the country; Justice Sotomayor, in dissent, argued that talking to a border agent at a legal crossing point is itself the first step of arrival. The practical effect is to clear the way for the government to revive "metering," turning asylum seekers away at ports of entry before they're ever inspected. Metering was first used under the Obama administration, expanded nationwide under Trump's first term, and rescinded by Biden in 2021. This time, it comes with the Court's blessing. Notice how narrow the ruling actually is. It applies to one specific group: people who are still on the Mexican side of an official crossing and are requesting entry. It says nothing about someone who has already crossed the border between checkpoints and is standing on US soil when an agent finds them. Legally, those are different questions. At Prolific, we decided to field a survey the following week, 2–3 July, among 1,500 US adults. At its core, this was an experiment testing whether it's where someone is, or why they're fleeing, that actually drives whether Americans think they deserve a hearing. Since the Court had already ruled, we added a second step. After respondents gave their initial answer, we described the real decision to them and asked again, to check something specific: do people change their minds once they've been told the Supreme Court has ruled on something? What we did Every respondent read about the same specific person, a 34-year-old woman from Guatemala asking for protection in the US. We randomly varied two things about her: where she was when she asked to start the asylum process, and why she was asking. That lets us separate whether attitudes toward asylum seekers depend on the reason, the location, or both. Specifically: Where she is. Either she is waiting at an official border crossing on the Mexican side and has not entered the US, or she has already crossed between checkpoints and was found by agents shortly after entering US territory. Why she is fleeing. Either she says she's fleeing political persecution, having received death threats after speaking out against corruption and gangs, or she says she's fleeing persecution over her gender identity, as a transgender woman who says Guatemalan authorities won't protect her. Around 375 people saw each of the four versions, and nobody saw more than one. We asked whether they thought she should be allowed to start the asylum process (not whether she should get asylum, just whether her case should be heard). After they answered, we described the real Supreme Court ruling, accurately and in plain language, and asked the same question again about the same person. Why someone is fleeing matters more than how they got here Before we mentioned the ruling at all, we asked people a simple question. Should this woman be allowed to start the asylum process? If public opinion followed the same logic as the law, where she's standing should matter quite a bit, but it didn't. When she was fleeing political persecution, support was high and barely moved with her location. 80.9% said yes while she waited at an official crossing, and 81.8% said yes once she'd already crossed the border for the same reason. Switch the reason to persecution over her gender identity, and support fell substantially, but again barely moved with location. 67.7% at an official crossing, 65.9% after already crossing. Putting those two comparisons side by side, we can see that political persecution draws 14 to 16 points more support than gender-identity persecution, and that gap holds almost exactly regardless of her location. The variable on which the Supreme Court's ruling is actually built, location, barely changes anyone's mind. The reason for fleeing does. Before we'd even told people about the ruling, Americans were already answering a different question than the one the Court had just answered. Not where she is, but why she's running. Republicans' support for asylum depends on why someone is fleeing We also wanted to see whether this varied by party identification. It does, and in a pretty informative way. For Democrats, support barely changes across scenarios; the difference here is bigger than sampling noise. Regardless of where the asylum seeker is, or why she's fleeing, around 90% of Democrats support her being able to start the asylum process. Now look at Republicans, and it's a completely different story. If she's fleeing for political reasons, between 71% and 76% of Republicans say she should be allowed to start the process, regardless of where she is. But if she's fleeing because being transgender puts her at risk, support drops to 33% at an official crossing, and 40% after she's already crossed. What about Independents? Do they sit closer to Democrats, closer to Republicans, or somewhere in between? It's a bit more complicated than that. On political persecution, they're close to Republicans. 78% would let her start the process at an official crossing, almost identical to the 79% after she's crossed. On gender identity, Independents do something neither party does. At the official crossing, 71% support her, well above Republicans' 33% and close to Democrats. But once she's already crossed the border, that falls to 58%, still a majority, but a 21-point drop from the 79% who'd support her in that same situation due to political persecution. Republicans, over that same shift, move slightly in the other direction, up from 33% to 40%. Independents are the only group whose answer depends on where the asylum seeker is, once the claim is about gender identity, and they move in the opposite direction from Republicans while doing it. Put together, this isn't simply that Republicans are tougher on asylum across the board. It's that the parties agree almost entirely when the reason isn't part of the current political debate, and disagree sharply when it is. The party gap in this experiment is about how people feel about transgender people. Independents are the exception, as their answer depends on both the reason and the location, unlike anyone else's. We described the ruling and support fell, even for the legal scenario After answering the initial question, we explained the Supreme Court's ruling and asked again whether the same woman should be allowed to initiate the asylum process. We hypothesized that, for respondents shown the official-crossing scenarios, the ruling should push some people from 'yes' to 'no', since those are the cases it actually covers. For respondents shown the already-crossed scenarios, we expected the ruling to barely register, since, on paper, her situation isn't affected by it at all. However, support fell across every scenario, not only those to which the ruling actually applies. Among the official-crossing scenarios, support for the woman fleeing political persecution dropped from 80.9% to 69.5% (down 11.4 points), and support for the woman fleeing gender-identity persecution dropped from 67.7% to 58.6% (down 9.1 points), exactly what we'd expected. But support for the woman who had already crossed the border fell by almost exactly as much: from 81.8% to 70.5% for political persecution (down 11.3 points), and from 65.9% to 56.3% for gender-identity persecution (down 9.6 points). The ruling only applies to people still waiting at an official crossing. Someone who has already set foot in the US isn't covered by the "haven't arrived" logic at all; her situation remains, on paper, exactly as legally valid a basis for asylum as it was before the ruling. Yet opinion moved almost identically, a 9-to-11-point swing against her, regardless of whether the ruling had anything to do with her situation. What explains that? One plausible reading is that people aren't treating the ruling as a narrow decision about who, under what circumstances, can start the asylum process. They're treating it as a signal that it's now acceptable to let people start the process at all. The ruling doesn't just carve out one legal exception; it puts turning people away back on the table as something the law permits. And once it's on the table, people seem to apply that logic well past the specific case it was written for. The caveats This is just one survey, with roughly 375 respondents reading each vignette. That's enough to detect a pattern as big and consistent as the one described above. It is not enough to be precise about any single subgroup number. We also decided to make the scenarios more personal. Instead of asking vaguely about "an asylum seeker," we focused on one specific person that participants could picture. That makes the experiment feel more real and more human, but it also means the exact numbers depend on the choices we made, her age, gender, and country of origin. Ask about a different person, and people might well answer differently. What’s key for this experiment isn't the precise level of support, which could shift for a different kind of asylum seeker, but whether that support changes depending on where she is and why she's fleeing. The experiment shows that where she is barely matters, but why she is fleeing does. After presenting the case, we told respondents about the Supreme Court's ruling. The results justify that choice, the ruling does change people's opinion, and the experiment lets us quantify how much. But because the ruling we described was real, decided a week before we fielded, some respondents' "before" answer may already have been shaped by news coverage they'd seen before our survey ever mentioned it. Our before/after comparison measures the effect of us explaining the ruling on top of whatever people already knew, not the effect of the ruling existing in a world where nobody had heard of it yet. Another fair objection to the before-and-after results is that this is just a measurement artifact. Maybe some respondents didn't register which scenario they'd read, and drifted along with whatever the ruling implied. That's worth checking directly, so we did in two ways. Restricting the analysis to only respondents who could accurately recall which scenario they'd read (which was most of them), the drop in support barely changes, shifts of a point or two at most. And testing directly whether failing the attention check predicts someone's opinion, once you control for which scenario they saw, it doesn't. The effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero, both before and after the ruling. It holds up even once you restrict it to people who read the scenario correctly. Do you want to use this data for reporting, academic work, or something else? Contact oriol.jover@prolific.com to discuss potential collaborations. Methodology: Prolific surveyed 1,500 US adults on 2–3 July 2026 using quotas for age, sex, and region. Results for the headline (scenario-level) figures were weighted to the US adult population on age × sex, race/ethnicity, region, education × age, housing tenure, and 2024 presidential vote via ranking. The party-ID breakdown reported later in this piece uses unweighted models with demographic controls; see the methods note above for why. Respondents were randomly assigned to one of four experimental scenarios (n≈375 each) and read a single version before answering. [EDIT: add Prolific's polling-transparency/registration line here if there's a US equivalent to the UK's BPC membership — didn't want to guess] The four scenarios respondents read were: Official crossing, political persecution: A 34-year-old woman from Guatemala traveled to the US-Mexico border and presented herself at an official border crossing, asking US border officials for protection. She is waiting on the Mexican side of the crossing. She has not entered the United States. She says she is fleeing because she received death threats after speaking publicly against corruption and the influence of criminal gangs in local politics. She says she cannot safely return to Guatemala. Official crossing, gender identity persecution: A 34-year-old transgender woman from Guatemala traveled to the US-Mexico border and presented herself at an official border crossing, asking US border officials for protection. She is waiting on the Mexican side of the crossing. She has not entered the United States. She says she is fleeing because she is transgender and has received threats and harassment because of her gender identity. She says the authorities in Guatemala would not protect her, and she cannot safely return. Already crossed, political persecution: A 34-year-old woman from Guatemala crossed the US-Mexico border between official checkpoints and was found by US border agents shortly after entering US territory. She told the agents that she wanted to apply for asylum in the United States. She says she is fleeing because she received death threats after speaking publicly against corruption and the influence of criminal gangs in local politics. She says she cannot safely return to Guatemala. Already crossed, gender identity persecution: A 34-year-old transgender woman from Guatemala crossed the US-Mexico border between official checkpoints and was found by US border agents shortly after entering US territory. She told the agents that she wanted to apply for asylum in the United States. She says she is fleeing because she is transgender and has received threats and harassment because of her gender identity. She says the authorities in Guatemala would not protect her, and she cannot safely return. After answering once, all respondents read the following before answering again: "In June 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled that people waiting on the Mexican side of an official border crossing have not legally 'arrived' in the United States for the purpose of applying for asylum. This means that the US government can turn people away at the border before they can start the asylum process, because legally they are not actually in the US."

title: Should Your Marketing Team Use NPS to Measure Event Engagement?
summary: This is why some event marketing teams are turning to the tried-and-true metric of NPS to capture and measure event engagement.
body_text: For years, organizations have been using NPS (Net Promoter Score) to measure customer sentiment and experience. NPS measures the likelihood a customer would recommend an organization, brand, product, or service to others, and then this score can be translated into a reading of the customer’s experience. For marketing teams, capturing event attendee engagement and/or experience has traditionally been challenging to achieve. There are so many different attendee touchpoints throughout an event that pinpointing which one translates closest to ‘attendee engagement’ isn’t as easy as one would hope. This is why some event marketing teams are turning to the tried-and-true metric of NPS to capture and measure event engagement. How to measure NPS Moving forward, we’ll be looking at NPS in relation to marketing events. So, the one question that you will have to ask your event attendees is: “On a scale of 0 – 10, how likely are you to recommend [this event] to a friend or peer?” Asking this one straightforward question gives your attendees the chance to reflect on their time spent at your event (Did they enjoy themselves? Did they learn anything?), any costs associated with the event (Was it worth it?), and their overall experience (Would someone I know enjoy this?). Once you have a pile of answers in hand, you can separate your responses into three main categories: 9 – 10 = promoters. These are people who enjoyed your event and would gladly recommend it to a peer. 7 – 8 = passives. These attendees probably enjoyed their time at your event but really wouldn’t recommend it to someone else. 0 – 6 = detractors. These people did not enjoy their time and would not recommend your event. To calculate your actual NPS, the formula = % promoters minus % detractors. Looking at the difference in the percentage of promotors and percentage of detractors from across your entire attendee population will give you your NPS ‍ Should you use NPS to measure event engagement? Now that you know how to calculate NPS, it’s time to figure out if you should use this number to determine event attendee engagement and experience. NPS is a best-practice, recognized metric that is understood across departments, ideologies, and industries. NPS is a clear go-to if you are looking for a number that can be easily understood by executives, board members, or other departments. In addition, your attendees will often recognize an NPS survey for what it is, giving them even more sway in how they answer this pointed question. On the other hand, event engagement pulls in from various factors, including but not limited to NPS. Your team should still track other engagement metrics such as conversations, demo requests, Q&A outreach, etc., to build a complete picture of event engagement. The bottom line? It never hurts to measure NPS. While your NPS may not be a completely clear measurement of attendee engagement, it can tell you how likely attendees are to attend an event in the future or recommend it to a colleague, which can help with planning and strategy for your future events.
